title: Effect of Al on the Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of High Carbon Lightweight Bearing Steel
abstract: Abstract The evolution of microstructures and mechanical properties in high carbon lightweight bearing steels with different Al contents was systematically studied. The results demonstrated that with increasing Al content, the ferrite fraction in the matrix gradually rose. In 10-wt pct Al steel, ferrite could not be fully eliminated even after austenitizing at 1150 °C, primarily due to a significant elevation in the austenitizing temperature. Regarding precipitate evolution, aluminum strongly facilitated the nucleation and growth of  κ -carbides, which competitively suppressed the formation of conventional M 3 C cementite. In addition, due to the variation of solubility of Al in austenite, the decreased Al solubility in austenite promotes ferrite precipitation along prior austenite grain boundaries, leading to a feather-like morphology. The local Al depletion simultaneously lowers the Ms temperature in the affected zones, thereby suppressing the martensite transition in these regions. Notably, lenticular martensite was initially observed in Fe–Cr–Al–C steel, primarily attributed to grain coarsening and elevated martensitic transformation stress induced by substantial Al addition. In terms of mechanical properties, the hardness of 6 and 8 wt pct Al steels was primarily governed by ferrite content, both reaching peak values of approximately 60 HRC at 900 °C and 1050 °C, respectively. The 10-wt pct Al steel failed to achieve a fully martensitic structure, resulting in lower hardness. In terms of toughness, the attainable peak impact energy of 6-wt pct Al steel significantly surpassed that of 8- and 10-wt pct Al steels, mainly attributed to its high grain boundary density, optimal ferrite fraction, and lath martensite structure. This study highlights a novel strategy of lightweight bearing steel by optimizing the added Al content and its consequent microstructure.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: As key components in mechanical transmission system, bearings are playing a very important role in the operation of mechanical equipment from aircraft to high-speed train. Generally, bearings with a rotational speed factor D m *N (D m : the diameter of a bearing in mm, N: rotational speed of a bearing in round per minute) value of higher than 2 * 10 6  mm*r/min are defined as ultra high-speed bearings. [ 1 ]  The high-speed rotation condition not only puts forward higher requirements on the room temperature mechanical properties, but also higher requirements on the high-temperature mechanical properties due to the rise of temperature caused by continuous friction.

Hardness was one of the most important mechanical properties of bearing steel. It is generally accepted that the hardness required for reliable operation of rolling bearing steel is about 58HRC. [ 2 ]  Generally, hardness of bearing steel will decrease as servicing temperature rise. For example, as the most widely used high-speed bearing steel at present, hardness of AISI 52100 will decrease sharply when servicing temperature rise to higher than 160 °C, therefore, the ultimate service temperature of AISI 52100 bearing steel is no higher than 160 °C. [ 3 ]  At higher temperature, the hardness of AISI 52100 will drop sharply, which will fail to meet the service requirements and cause failure.

Previous researches [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ]  had shown that aluminum can significantly improve the stability of high-temperature mechanical properties of a high carbon bearing steel, therefore, alloyed with aluminum to existing composition systems such as high carbon chromium bearing steel systems becomes an important strategy [ 7 ]  for bearing steels designed for servicing at elevated temperature. The improved mechanical properties were brought by various iron aluminides. [ 5 ]  However, as a novel compositional system, the mechanism of how Al affects microstructure of steel and its optimal addition level still remain to be deeply elucidated. [ 4 , 8 ]

As a ferrite-stabilizing element, the addition of aluminum can expand the ferrite phase region and narrow the austenite region in the phase diagram. At the same time, it has been reported that excessive aluminum content can introduce δ-ferrite into steel, [ 9 ]  which is harmful to the toughness of steel. In addition, aluminum can form a new type of carbide with Fe and C, which is AlFe 3 C x  ( x  = 0.5–1), also known as  κ  carbides. [ 8 ] κ  carbides tend to form at grain boundaries in ferritic steels and is relatively large in size, which can be detrimental to the mechanical properties of steel. [ 10 ]  When content of Al was below about 20 at. pct, the matrix was regarded as a A2 disordered solution phase. Only when the content of Al in a binary alloy comes to higher than at least 20 at. pct will the B2(AlFe) or D03(AlFe 3 ) phase be seen in the alloy. In addition, interaction between Al with steel with a content of C higher than 1.0 wt pct has not been studied further. In the case, whether carbon contributes to the formation of aluminides still remains unclear. At the same time, decisive results on the content of aluminum in helping composition design are still lacking. In addition, there are still many issues to be addressed, such as the effect of Al on martensite structure, retained austenite (RA) and precipitates, as well as the effect of Al on the toughness of steel.

To address the issues mentioned above, a series of new alloys with aluminum content of 6, 8 and 10 wt pct were designed to verify the effects of higher aluminum content on the microstructure and properties of lightweight high-carbon chromium bearing steel system. We mainly studied the microstructure and mechanical properties with various methods under different heat treatment experiments of high-carbon chromium bearing steels with different aluminum contents. This paper mainly focused on the evolution of martensite, RA and precipitates, so as to elucidate the effect of Al on the microstructure evolution and its underlying mechanism.

sections.heading: Preparation of Steel
paragraphs: Thermodynamic phase diagrams of the three materials were calculated through Thermo-Calc firstly. Subsequently, a series of high-aluminum, high-carbon chromium bearing steels with nominal compositions of Fe−1.2C– x Al–1.5Cr (where  x  = 6, 8, 10) were melted  via  vacuum melting, with poured ingot weighting about 50 kg. Samples were then taken from the riser for compositional analysis, and the results of the main compositions both in wt pct and at. pct are listed in the following Table  I . All three ingots were forged under the same process. The ingots were scalped and then homogenized at 1150 °C for 5 hours. Immediately after being removed from the furnace, they were forged with the final forging temperature controlled above 950 °C. After upsetting, the workpieces were forged out along the  Z -axis, with each pass having a deformation of about 50 pct. The final dimensions of the forged bars were approximately 70 × 70 × 1000 mm. After forging, the bars were air-cooled to room temperature.

sections.heading: Heat Treatment Process
paragraphs: After forging, the forged bars of the three steels were subjected to stress-relief annealing by holding at 850 °C for 2 hours. To accurately determine the Ac1 and Ac3 temperatures of the materials to assist with the heat treatment experiments, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) tests were conducted on the three steels separately, with the results shown in Figure  1 . The DSC results indicated that the Ac1–Ac3 temperatures for the three materials were 834 °C to 935 °C, 895 °C to 1042 °C, and 960 °C to 1101 °C, respectively. Based on these results, heat treatment parameters were selected for quenching. For the 6Al composition, four austenitizing temperatures were chosen around 935 °C, namely 850 °C to 1000 °C. Since the Ac3 temperatures for the 8Al and 10Al compositions were higher, the austenitizing temperatures for these two samples were selected within the range of 1000 °C to 1150 °C. After quenching, tempering was conducted with the primary aim of reducing quenching stress. During the heat treatment process, a strategy of loading the samples into the furnace when the target temperature was reached was adopted. Heat treatment process route after forging was shown in Figure  2 . Fig. 1 DSC results of three steels Fig. 2 Heat treatment regime for high-aluminum bearing steels

sections.heading: Methods for Characterization and Test
paragraphs: Scanning electron microscope (SEM) and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) were both conducted on a MIRA 3 TESCAN field emission gun. SEM used secondary electron imaging with a 20-kV accelerating voltage. Samples used for SEM were all cut from heat-treated samples by wire cut electrical discharge machining (WEDM) and were sanded and polished before etched. Samples for EBSD were cut and sanded in the same way as SEM samples with a thickness of 5 mm, but were further polished with 50-nm colloidal silica after polished with 1- μ m diamond paste. The accelerating voltage and probe current used in EBSD were 20 kV and 5 nA, respectively. EBSD data were processed with Crystal software.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) experiments were conducted on a Smart Lab 9kw instruments from Rigaku Corporation with a Cu tube. X-ray scans were performed over 30 to 90 deg range at the scan rate of 3 °/min. Samples for XRD were prepared in the same way as EBSD samples. Patterns were analyzed with the MDI Jade software. Micro-strain distribution was calculated with Debye–Scherrer equation.

For tensile tests, the tensile specimens were measured M10 ×  φ 4, and with three parallel samples per group. The impact specimens were 10 × 10 × 55 mm unnotched bars, also in sets of three. Hardness was determined by Rockwell testing and three indents were made on each specimen.

sections.heading: Annealing State
paragraphs: The SEM images of the three steels in the annealed state after forging are shown in Figure  3  and the corresponding energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) line scanning results are shown in Figure  4 . It was apparent that in Figure  3 , there were two kinds of precipitates, one is with higher brightness than the matrix and the other one is with lower brightness. According to the EDS line scan results in Figure  4 , the bright precipitates were rich in Cr and the dark precipitates were rich in Al, respectively. XRD results of all three steels were shown in Figure  5  and peaks of  κ  carbides and M 3 C ( M  = Cr, Fe) were matched through Jade.  κ  carbide was the only Al-rich phase in the steel and M 3 C ( θ  carbide) was the only possible Cr-rich phase. Therefore, the dark Al-rich carbides and bright Cr-rich carbides were  κ  carbides and M 3 C, respectively. In Figures  3 (a) and (c), it was obvious that  κ  carbides were generally bigger than M 3 C, which was attributed to the higher content of the main forming element Al for  κ  carbide. As content of Al came to 10 wt pct, blocky  κ  carbides got far larger than that in 6Al. Fig. 3 SEM pictures of annealed steel obtained under BSE, ( a ) through ( c ): 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al Fig. 4 EDS line scanning results of ( a ): 6Al, ( b ) 8Al, and ( c ):10Al.  κ  and  θ  referred to  κ  carbides and M 3 C, respectively Fig. 5 XRD profiles of annealed steels of 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al

The total amount of  κ -carbides increased significantly with the increasing aluminum content, and a similar trend was observed in their average size. The formation of large blocky  κ  carbides were attributed to the annealing process during which Oswald ripening happened [ 11 ]  thoroughly and therefore carbides grew larger. Given that the annealing temperature was set at 850 °C, only the 6Al steel reached its Ac1 temperature, which implied that dissolution of carbides and transformation from ferrite to austenite occurred. During holding at 850 °C, spheroidization process happed gradually. In contrast, for the 8Al and 10Al steels, the holding temperature did not reach the Ac1 temperature, resulting in only the growth of carbides without any significant change in their shape. In 8Al and 10Al steels, higher aluminum content significantly promoted the growth of  κ -carbides which led to a substantial reduction in the formation of M 3 C carbides in the matrix, because the  κ -carbides occupied a large amount of carbon, thereby reducing the driving force for the formation of M 3 C.

sections.heading: Precipitates and matrix evolution
paragraphs: Firstly, to figure out the phase composition of steels, XRD experiments were conducted on steels after austenitizing under different quenching and corresponding results are shown in Figure  6 . In Figure  6 (a), peaks of ferrite were found to decrease gradually and disappear in 6Al-1000. For  κ  carbides, peaks of them disappeared in 6Al-900Q. In Figure  6 (b), no apparent peaks of ferrite were found in the profile of 1050 °C, in which all ferrite transformed into martensite. In addition, no peaks of precipitates were found in all four states. In Figure  6 (c), unlike other steels which had pure ferrite peaks, there was a weak peak overlapped with the (110) peak of ferrite around 2 θ  = 44.35 deg. According to powder diffraction (PDF) database, the side peak was possibly peak of AlFe or AlFe 3  phase. In the result of Martin Palm  et al. , [ 5 ]  AlFe 3  had a lower request on the content of Al compared to AlFe phase at room temperature. Hence, the phase was concluded to be AlFe 3 . In high Mn steel or medium Mn steel with an austenite matrix, [ 12 , 13 ]  D03 phase or B2 phase was easy to be distinguished from the matrix because they had clear boundaries with face-centered cubic (FCC) matrix. In this study, it is on the contrary, no apparent phase was seen in the SEM pictures shown in Figure  7 ; this was mainly caused by the very close lattice parameter between D03 phase and ferrite matrix, which means that they could have fully coherent interface. Fig. 6 XRD profiles of three steels austenitizing at different temperatures, ( a ) through ( c ): 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al Fig. 7 Quenching microstructure of steel 6Al, 8Al, and 10Al, ( a1 ) through ( a4 ): 6Al and 850 °C to 1000 °C; ( b1 ) through ( b4 ): 8Al, 1000 °C to 1150 °C; ( c1 ) through ( c4 ): 10Al, 1000 °C to 1150 °C

The microstructures of three steels after quenching under different conditions are shown in Figure  7 . For all steels austenitizing at different temperatures, samples were numbered as Al content and austenitizing temperature like 6Al-900. To aid in identifying the phases present in steel under different heat treatments, EDS line scanning experiments were conducted, and the results are shown in Figure  8 , in which  α ,  α ′, and  κ  refer to ferrite, martensite and  κ  carbides, respectively. In Figure  8 (a), 8Al-1000, the etched area was depleted in C but rich in Al, it was therefore identified as ferrite. In Figure  8 (b), 10Al-1100, the precipitates were rich in both C and Al, they were identified as  κ  carbides. Identification of  α  and  α ′ were in the same way as in Figure  8 (a). In Figure  8 (c), 10Al-1150, the round flat area was lack of C but rich in Al. On the boundary, the bright particles were rich in both carbon and Al, they were regarded as  κ  carbides. While in Figure  8 (d), it was found that the boundary of the etched block area had higher content of Al and C, there were regarded as  κ  carbide, therefore. For the blocky area, they were found to be rich in Fe and almost the same content of Al and lower content of C than the matrix on two sides. Fig. 8 ( a ) 8Al austenitizing at 1000 °C; ( b ) 10Al austenitizing at 1100 °C; ( c ) and ( d ) 10Al austenitizing at 1150 °C

In Figures  7 (a1) through (a4) M 3 C and  κ  carbides both dissolved into austenite gradually as temperature rises. In Figures  7 (b1) through (b4), the higher content of Al rose the full austenite temperature and thus ferrite did not transform until 1050 °C. Another obvious change needed to be mentioned was the changing characteristic of martensite plates. In 6Al-1000, the martensite plates did not show a parallel structure; therefore, they were regarded as V shaped structure. In 8Al-1100, the alternating two martensite plates exhibited parallel structural features. Therefore, martensite plates in Figures  7 (b3) and (b4) were denoted as zigzag structure. The higher content of Al changed the shearing angle of transformation of martensite from austenite. As content of Al increased to be 10 wt pct, in which the atomic percent of Al was about 17.93 at. pct, the fully dissolved temperature of  κ  carbides were far higher than 8Al steel.  κ  carbides keep incompletely dissolved till 1150 °C. At 1050 °C to 1100 °C,  κ  carbide showed a partial dissolved and reprecipitation process. The small bright particles appeared at the ferrite boundary were identified to be  κ  carbides in the following EDS results shown in Figures  8 (b) and (c). Generally, higher content of Al lifted the dissolving temperature of  κ  carbides.

Due to the varied solid solubility limit of Al in steel [ 14 , 15 ]  as temperature change,  κ  carbides faced a dissolved and reprecipitate process. In heating process, large-sized  κ  carbides could not fully dissolved into matrix, as shown in Figures  7 (c1) and (c2), part of them reserved until a higher temperature. In the flowing quenching process after soaking, part of the dissolved Al atoms precipitated as tiny  κ  carbides around the prior austenite–ferrite boundaries. The reprecipitated  κ  carbides had little time to grow up, therefore they were far smaller than the annealed ones.

Generally, higher content of Al stabilized  κ  carbides much and lifted the dissolving point of  κ -carbides much, from 850 °C to 900 °C in 6Al steel to 1050 °C to 1100 °C in 10Al steel. The solvus limit of Al in steel lifted the Ac3 temperature, made the full austenite temperature of steel increase from 950 °C to 1050 °C and lastly higher than 1100 °C when content of Al varied from 6 to 10 wt pct. Structure of  κ  carbides in steel with different contents of Al keep unchanged in researched system, this consisted with the results of other researchers. [ 16 , 17 ]

Higher content of Al in steel introduced AlFe 3  phase into the matrix. At present, seldom research focused on the AlFe 3  phase in ferrite steel or martensite steel, some researchers reported the effect of AlFe 3  phase on microstructure and mechanical properties on austenite steel manufactured in various methods. [ 18 , 19 ]  Their results showed that AlFe 3  was easier to distinguish in austenite steel. This was because AlFe 3  was of BCC structure and austenite had the structure of FCC. However, in the present steel, due to the similar crystal structure between ferrite and AlFe 3  phase, it was hard to distinguish them with EBSD method. It was possible that they even share an elastically strained coherent orientation relationship and that is why we could not observe their boundaries in SEM pictures. Although peaks besides the main peaks of ferrite were observed indeed, it was still hard to ensure the distribution of AlFe 3 .

For content of RA, when content of Al varied from 6 to 8 wt pct, the formation of RA was retarded. Especially for 8Al austenitizing at 1100 °C, almost no peaks of RA were found in Figure  6 (b). However, as content of Al rises to 10 wt pct, effect of Al on RA altered. Due to the formation of much AlFe 3 , content of Al dissolved into austenite was less than that in 8Al steel, and therefore, there were much RA in the quenched steel. In contrast, the content of RA did not show the expected trend.

sections.heading: Lenticular martensite
paragraphs: Figure  9  illustrates the BC map, IPF map, and phase map acquired from EBSD data. In fact, martensite in the present steel belonged to plate martensite. In some occasions, as the tips of plates got far thinner than the middle part, it was also called lenticular martensite. [ 20 ]  Their difference mainly lied in the width of branches of the zigzag structure or twinning area. As for the corners of martensite plates, they showed a triangular characteristic in Figures  9 (a1) through (a3) but the characteristics of a parallelogram in Figures  9 (b1) through (b3). In the triangular region in 6Al-1000, plates from both sides of large plates would conflict, which introduced a transformation resistance from austenite to martensite plates. As for parallelogram in Figures  9 (b1) through (b3), the secondary plates in the primary plate corners seemed to inherit the orientation characteristics of the primary plates, which made the nucleation sites for branches densely distributed along the plate boundaries. The adequate nucleation sites made it less possible to form RA. This explained the disappearance of peaks of RA in Figure  6 (b). Fig. 9 BC map, IPF map and phase map of: 6Al-1000Q ( a1 ) through ( a3 ); 8Al-1100Q ( b1 ) through ( b3 ); and 10Al-1150Q ( c1 ) through ( c3 )

At present, the formation of zigzag structure was attributed to the burst nucleation of martensite. The burst nucleation of martensite was thought to be caused by both chemical factors and inner stress factor. [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ]  Due to the rapid cooling, it is almost impossible for the spread of Al atoms during quenching, which means that the plate corner had the same composition as the martensite plates. In addition, there exists kernel average misorientation (KAM) difference observed between martensite plates as shown in Figure  10 . In the KAM map, the neighboring plates had different KAM values while the intermittent plates had similar KAM values, which was because that they belonged to different variants. In the plate corner, the KAM value on the tip of plates was far higher than in the plate, which means a high inner stress retained around the tip of plates. Therefore, it is concluded that the formation of burst nucleation of martensite was mainly caused by the stress mechanism. Fig. 10 BC map ( a ) and KAM map ( b ) of 8Al steel quenched at 1100 °C

In this study, the formation mechanism of lenticular martensite can be summarized as follows: after a martensite plate nucleated, the midrib [ 20 ]  of it grew far faster than the twins. When the midrib of a plate reaches the grain boundary, there would be a stress field on the end of a tip, which caused the nucleation of a martensite plate. The newly formed martensite plate would continue forming and induce nucleation process. The fast spread rate of martensite midribs making the plates inside the same martensite were induced from only a few martensite nuclei. The inherited orientation relationship between martensite plates, the orientation of martensite plates within the same original austenite grain is relatively uniform. In Figure  9 (b2), the martensite had only two orientations in the observed area.

It is worth noting that, the burst nucleation process was only observed in the Fe–Ni–C system. [ 24 , 25 ]  Here, it was the first time that the burst nucleation of martensite was observed in a new composition system. For research on the nucleation process of the Fe–Ni–C system, researchers primarily focused on martensite variants [ 25 , 26 ]  rather than the nucleation mechanism. Due to the rapid nucleation and growth of martensite plates, research on the nucleation of martensite was scarce.

sections.heading: Feather-like structure and AlFe 3
paragraphs: In Figures  9 (c1) through (c3), there were a large number of unresolved areas, corresponding to the widened peaks of martensite in Figure  6 (c). The severely broadened peaks indicated a significant deviation of the lattice parameters from the standard values, which led to difficulties in obtaining resolvable Kikuchi patterns while conducting EBSD experiments. Except from the dense dislocation density, the filiform acicular martensite plates in the high density of dislocation area were also a reason for the broadening of peaks of martensite. Only in BC map could the martensite plates be observed.

For 10Al steel austenitized at 1150 °C, generally, it could be divided into three areas: the feather-like area, spherical area, and martensite area. In Figure  9 (c2), FCC phase in branches intervals on both sides of the stem had different orientations, therefore, it was inferred that they belonged to different prior austenite grains. The feather-like structure distributed around the boundary of prior austenite grains. The spherical area was identified as AlFe 3  in the follow results according to the EDS results.

Figure  11  shows the BC map, phase map, and corresponding EDS results around a feather-like structure area. It was shown that branches of feather-like structure were apparently rich in Fe and Al but lack of C. In comparison with spherical area, the branches owned lower content of Al but higher content of Cr element. Hence, although the branches and spherical areas were both BCC phases and branches near the spherical area had the same orientation with spherical areas, they were still regarded as different phases due to the different elemental concentrations. The spherical BCC phase enriched in Al was identified as AlFe 3  and the feather-like BCC phase was identified as ferrite. Fig. 11 BC map, IPF map, and phase map of 10Al-1150 and corresponding EDS map of Fe, Cr, Al, and C

A schematic diagram was drawn to illustrate the forming mechanism of feather-like structure and spherical AlFe 3  phase as shown in Figure  12 . Figure  12  illustrates the thermal cycle of the 10Al steel, involving heating from room temperature to approximately 1150 °C followed by quenching. 1) Stage 1 represents the microstructure at room temperature. 2) In Stage 2, partial dissolution of carbides is observed, accompanied by the austenitization of the adjacent matrix. 3) Stage 3 indicates the complete austenitization of the matrix. 4) In Stage 4, the steel undergoes cooling; the microstructure depicts the hypothesized state at a temperature slightly below Ar3, characterized by the precipitation of interfacial ferrite. 5) Stage 5 displays the final as-quenched microstructure, which consists of martensite, interfacial ferrite, adjacent retained austenite, and residual AlFe 3  intermetallic compounds. While heating, the large-sized  κ  carbides confronted a gradual dissolution process.  κ  carbides had large size, which made it impossible for the entire single carbide dissolved, as shown in Figures  7 (c2) through (c3). After  κ  carbides fully dissolved into the matrix, due to the limitation of solubility of Al in the austenite matrix, there were spherical Al-rich regions remained. The Al-rich region would transform to AlFe 3  phase in the subsequent cooling process. As cooling proceeding, solubility of Al in austenite decreased, [ 5 ]  Al around grain boundaries of austenite start to migrating together and promoting the formation of ferrite. While steel reached the critical temperature, ferrite started to nucleate and grow. In the last, when the temperature reached the Ms point of 10Al steel, the inner austenite transformed to martensite and austenite around prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs) would preserve till the transformation finished. The retention of austenite around the PAGBs was primarily attributed to the precipitation of Al in the form of ferrite or AlFe 3 . In contrast, 8Al steel at quenched state owned a special fractal structure to cut down the transformation stress very well and in turn had little austenite retained in the matrix. Fig. 12 Schematic diagram of the forming mechanism of feather-like structure and spherical AlFe 3  phase in 10Al steel during heating and quenching processes

sections.heading: Strength
paragraphs: For bearing steel, hardness and strength were two primary static mechanical properties. [ 2 , 3 ]  The deformability of 8 and 10Al steels was so poor that tensile samples fractured before yielding. Therefore, it was hard to acquired yield strength of these steels. [ 27 , 28 ]  For the present steel, only the ultimate tensile strength was collected. The tensile strength steel is shown in Figure  13 . Fig. 13 Tensile strength of all three steels austenitizing at different temperatures

For 6Al steel, samples austenitized at 900 °C exhibited the highest tensile properties. In comparison with steels treated at higher temperatures, specimens austenitizing under this condition had the finest prior austenite grain (PAG) and the highest volume fraction of strengthening phases as shown in Figures  7 (a1) through (a4); compared with 6Al-850 they also possess a higher content of martensite. These factors contributed to the optimal tensile properties. For 8Al steel, tensile strength decreased monotonically with increasing austenitizing temperature. The decline attributed to the coarsening of PAG and the formation of large martensite laths. [ 29 ]  As for 10Al steel, the trend is different: samples austenitized at 1050 °C owned the highest tensile strength. Microstructure shown in Figures  7 (c1) and (c4) indicated that the pronounced reprecipitation of  κ -carbide was primarily contributor. The strengths of specimens austenitized at 1100 °C and 1150 °C are similar and both lower than that of the 10Al steel quenched from 1050 °C.

The strength loss caused by increasing the aluminum content to 8 wt pct was attributed to the fact that, as we argue, the prior austenite grain size and martensitic lath dimensions constitute the most critical determinants of strength. The strength of 6Al austenitized at 1000 °C was very close to the strength of 8Al steel austenitized at 1000 °C and 1050 °C, which meant that the strengthening effect of solid solution Al atoms had an positive effect on the tensile strength of steel.

In fact, the principal advantage of incorporating aluminum into high-carbon chromium bearing steels lies in the substantial optimization of their elevated temperature performance. Therefore, strength of 6Al and commercial 52100 bearing steel at elevated temperature was acquired and the results are shown in Figure  14 . 6Al had the most promising property, therefore, only strength of 6Al steel at elevated was acquired. Although the tensile strength (TS) of 52100 steel at room temperature was about 200 MPa higher than 6Al steel, the TS of 6Al steel was higher than 52100 steels when the servicing temperature was 200 °C. The strength of 52100 at 200 °C decreased by about 19 pct; however, for 6Al, the strength decreased only 11 pct. For strength at 300 °C, the strength of 52100 steel and 6Al decreased by 36 and 23 pct, respectively. In addition, the 6Al steel had higher yield strength (YS) at all test temperatures. Fig. 14 Tensile strength and yield strength of 6Al and 52100 bearing steel test at different temperatures
The aluminum-alloying strategy effectively suppresses the high-temperature strength degradation in high-carbon chromium bearing steels.

The impact energy of all three steels after heat treatment under respective process is shown in Figure  15 . For the 6Al steel, peak value of impact energy was reached at 900 °C and then decreased rapidly. The decline of toughness was attributed to the lack of carbides and larger PAG which resulted in bigger martensite plates. In addition, for bearing steels which had poor ductility, the Charpy impact energy essentially excludes any contribution from plastic-deformation work; accordingly, provided the influence of precipitates is disregarded, its value is dictated almost exclusively by the tensile strength. Consequently, the variation of impact energy with austenitizing temperature closely mirrors the evolution of tensile strength for 6Al steel. Fig. 15 Unnotched impact energy of 6 to 10Al steels under different processes

Generally, lenticular martensite had poor deformability and low fracture toughness, [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ]  this was mainly because of their high inner stress and solid solution C atoms and large plate size. Large plate size generally meant lower density of high-angle grain boundaries which was the main obstacle for the spread of cracks. In addition, solid solution Al atoms were detrimental to the deformability and toughness of steels, [ 33 , 34 ]  too. Al solution atoms lower the surface energy of steel [ 35 ]  and in turn lower the energy needed for the spread of fracture.

RA was always thought to be beneficial for the toughness of martensite steel; [ 36 ]  however, there was little RA in 8Al steel compared to 6Al steel and 10Al steel. The lack of RA was regarded as the main reason contribute to the poor toughness of 8Al steel. [ 37 ]  At the same time, for 8Al austenitizing at 1000 °C, due to the existence of ferrite, higher toughness than treated at other conditions was acquired.

For the 10Al steel, the impact energy peaked at 1100 °C as the austenitizing temperature increased. By comparing the microstructures under different austenitizing temperature, it was found that unlike the 8Al steel, 10Al steel under different condition contain a large amount of ferrite phase. The peak value was achieved at 1100 °C because of higher density of precipitations as shown in Figure  7 (c3). In comparison with 10Al-1150, 10Al-1100 had a lower content of martensite which was also indicated by hardness as shown in Figure  17 . As a whole, due to relatively higher content of soft phase and higher content of precipitates, 10Al steel austenitized at 1100 °C had a slightly higher toughness than austenitized at other temperature.

To further claim the strengthening mechanism of 6Al quenched from 900 °C, density of dislocation, effective grain size, and density of carbides were collected and shown in Figure  16 . Density of dislocation was calculated through the peak broadening of XRD data, and the other two were quantified through SEM pictures. Fig. 16 Density of dislocation and effective grain size of 6Al steel quenched from different temperatures

As shown in Figure  16 , 6Al steel quenched from 900 °C had the highest density of dislocation and finest grain size of about 4.09 * E15 m −2  and 2.4  μ m, respectively. Higher density of carbides of 6Al steel quenching from 850 °C will not compensate the strengthening effect of finer grain size of 6Al steel quenched from 900 °C. Therefore, 6Al steel austenitized from 900 °C had the optimal strength.

For brittle bearing steels, the crack-initiation work accounts for the dominant fraction of the total impact energy. Hence, the Charpy impact energy was generally proportional to the tensile strength of steels. Moreover, when it came to the resistance to crack propagation, grain boundaries and precipitates were the dominant factors. Although the 6Al steel quenched from 850 °C had a slightly higher number density of precipitate, however, it was insufficient to compensate for the much lower grain-boundary density compared with the steel quenched from 900 °C. Consequently, the 6Al steel quenched from 900 °C exhibits the highest impact energy, too. In addition, the higher content of RA also contributes to the highest toughness of 6Al steel compared to 6Al steel quenched from other condition.

sections.heading: Hardness
paragraphs: Hardness of bearing steels with different aluminum contents after quenching under respective conditions is shown in Figure  17 . For ferrous materials, hardness is directly determined by factors such as the content of hard phase, carbon content in the matrix and the content of carbides, and dislocation density. Hardness of 6Al steel is mainly determined by the content of martensite. As austenitizing temperature rose, volume percent of martensite increased gradually. In terms of 8Al steel, as martensite rose to higher than 95 pct while austenitized at 1050 °C, the hardness approached plateau. At this point, although there was a little of ferrite in the matrix, the content of solution carbon in the martensite was almost identical to that austenitized at higher temperature. The hardness of steel was mainly brought by the solid solution carbon atoms. As for 10Al steel, the high aluminum content increased the Ac3 temperature significantly. According to the DSC results in Figure  1 (c), austenitizing process had been finished at about 1100 °C. However, even austenitized at 1150 °C, a full martensite/austenite structure was not achieved. Also, it was obvious that there were much RA and ferrite as shown in Figure  11 (c3), which made the hardness of 10Al steel far lower than 8Al steel under the same austenitizing condition. Fig. 17 Hardness of 6 to 10Al steels after treated under different processes

Overall, it was easy for the 6Al steel and 8Al steel to satisfy the hardness requirement of bearing steel [ 2 ]  at acceptable condition. Due to the excessively high aluminum content, it was hard for 10Al steel to acquire a full martensite microstructure. In addition, it was speculated that ferrite precipitate from the austenite while cooling due to the solubility limit of Al in austenite. The formation mechanism of ferrite was similar with the formation process of ferrite in a hypoeutectoid steel. [ 38 ]  The distinction between the two phenomena primarily lay in the temporal window employed. More elements that would contribute to the formation of austenite or lower the Ac3 temperature of steel needed to be added to 10Al steel if one wants to design a full martensite microstructure with the same content of Al.

Typical hardness and impact energy of full-martensite 52100 was about 59-62HRC and 20 to 70 J, respectively. [ 39 ,  40 – 41 ]  For the toughness, the optimal value was about 35 J, which was about half of the well-treated 52100 bearing steel. For hardness, the 6Al steel was slightly lower than 52100 steels. However, the hardness of 6Al steel will increase after cryogenic and tempering treatment.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The evolution of microstructure in high carbon lightweight bearing steel with different Al contents was systematically studied, including the evolution of precipitates, lenticular martensite, AlFe 3  and retained austenite. The mechanism by which these microstructures affect the mechanical properties was discussed in depth. Based on the results, the following conclusions can be drawn: With increasing Al content, the Ac3 temperature rises significantly, leading to an increased ferrite fraction in the matrix. In 10-wt pct Al steel, ferrite cannot be fully eliminated even after austenitizing at 1150 °C. Regarding precipitates, aluminum markedly promotes the nucleation and growth of  κ -carbides, while competitively suppressing the formation of conventional M 3 C-type cementite. Lenticular martensite was initially observed in Fe–Cr–Al–C steel, primarily attributed to the substantial Al addition-induced grain coarsening and the elevated martensitic transformation stress, which promoted burst nucleation and led to the formation of zigzag lenticular martensite. 6Al steel quenched from 900 °C had the highest strength of 2261 MPa and impact energy of 35 J due to the tiny PAG and martensite plates. In terms of hardness, the hardness of 6 and 8Al steels were primarily governed by ferrite content, both reaching plateau values of approximately 60 HRC when quenching from 900 °C and 1050 °C, respectively. Even after austenitizing at 1150 °C and subsequent quenching, the microstructure of 10Al steel fails to transform fully into martensite; consequently, its hardness remained far lower than the general requirement specified for bearing steels. The addition of Al retarded the deterioration of strength of 52100 steel significantly, offering a new strategy to improve the strength of steel at elevated temperature.
